sections.title: Why interviewers ask you to estimate

blocks.text: Back-of-envelope estimation isn't about getting the exact number. It's about letting numbers drive design decisions: does the data fit on one machine? Do we need a cache? Is this read-heavy or write-heavy? Will one database handle the write rate? A two-minute estimate that says "~200 GB, fits in memory on a few nodes" can eliminate half the architecture you'd otherwise draw.
Interviewers want to see a **repeatable method**, sensible rounding, and — most importantly — what you conclude from the numbers. An estimate that doesn't change any decision is wasted time.

items.title: Users → actions
items.text: Start from DAU and actions per user per day: 100M DAU × 10 posts viewed = 1B reads/day.

items.title: Per day → per second
items.text: Divide by ~100k (86,400 s rounds to 10⁵): 1B/day ≈ 10k/s average.

items.title: Average → peak
items.text: Multiply by 2–5× for daily peaks, more for events (on-sales, New Year).

items.title: Storage
items.text: Writes/day × object size × retention × replication factor.

items.title: Bandwidth
items.text: QPS × response size, separately for ingress and egress.

items.title: Conclude
items.text: Compare against per-machine capacity and state the design consequence.

blocks.title: Key insight
blocks.text: Memorise one conversion: **1M per day ≈ 12 per second.** Everything else is multiplication.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: At ~6 GB/s of image egress the origin can't serve this; images go to object storage behind a CDN, and the app servers only serve metadata.

head: Component
Rough capacity per node
Implication
rows: Beyond that: replicas for reads, sharding for writes
One cluster handles most caching needs
Large media needs many nodes or a CDN

head: Operation
Time
So what
rows: 1,000× slower than RAM — cache hot data
A dozen sequential service calls add up

items: Components in **series** multiply: three 99.9% services in a chain ≈ 99.7%.
**Redundant** components in parallel: 1 − (1 − a)². Two independent 99% replicas ≈ 99.99%.
This is why every synchronous dependency you add lowers your ceiling.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Spending five minutes on precise arithmetic. Round aggressively (86,400 → 100k, 2.5 → 3) and say you're rounding.

items: Forgetting peak vs average — systems are sized for peak.
Forgetting replication (×3) and indexes (+30–50%) in storage.
Not converting units carefully (bits vs bytes on network links).
Estimating and then not using the result.
